subject: Biotechnology
title: Enzyme Replacement Therapy
description: A micro-lesson that makes Enzyme Replacement Therapy usable.

hook.text: Gaucher disease patients lack one enzyme — their cells fill with undigested fat, swelling liver and spleen.

buildup.text: Ceredase was the first enzyme replacement — purified from human placentas. It took 20,000 placentas per patient per year.

discovery.text: Cerezyme replaced it — recombinant glucocerebrosidase from CHO cells, unlimited supply without human tissue.

twist.text: ERT now treats Fabry, Pompe, and MPS disorders — but costs over $200,000 per patient per year.

climax.text: These drugs transformed fatal childhood diseases into manageable conditions — price is the remaining barrier.

punchline.text: Replace what the body cannot make — enzyme therapy is liquid rescue.

quiz.question: Why is enzyme replacement therapy so expensive?
options: The enzymes must be imported from only one country
Production requires complex mammalian cell culture and patient populations are very small
The enzymes degrade immediately and need continuous infusion

details.summary: Enzyme replacement therapy treats lysosomal storage disorders by supplying patients with the functional enzyme their bodies cannot produce. Regular intravenous infusions of recombinant enzymes like imiglucerase for Gaucher disease prevent organ damage and improve quality of life.
details.whyItMatters: ERT transformed fatal childhood diseases into manageable conditions. Gaucher disease treatment was biotech's early success story, proving that recombinant proteins could replace missing human enzymes and inspiring development of therapies for dozens
takeaways: ERT provides functional enzymes to patients with genetic enzyme deficiencies
It treats lysosomal storage disorders like Gaucher, Fabry, and Pompe disease
Patients require lifelong regular infusions costing hundreds of thousands annually

faq.question: Why do enzyme replacement therapies cost so much?
faq.answer: ERT drugs treat extremely rare diseases with tiny patient populations, preventing economies of scale. Manufacturing complex recombinant enzymes is expensive, and R&D costs must be recovered from few patients. Orphan drug incentives help but prices often exceed 200,000 dollars annually.

faq.question: Could gene therapy eventually replace enzyme replacement therapy?
faq.answer: Gene therapy could provide a one-time cure by enabling patients' cells to produce the missing enzyme permanently. Clinical trials for Fabry and Gaucher disease are underway. Success would eliminate the need for lifelong infusions, potentially reducing long-term costs.
